sentences.text: Will Thursday's update hold, or is the author still buried in revisions on the aftermath chapter? Talking about my mother for forty minutes when I'd come in to talk about the mornings. Tagged it "Heavy Themes" and "Mind the Warnings" because the last arc broke readers who skimmed. Fragile isn't the word; scraped clean is closer to how the drive home felt. Whoever recommended this fic to me owes me tissues, a nap, and an apology, in that exact order. What do you do with your face in a waiting room where everyone knows why everyone else is there? "Chapter 15 when," the comments demand, as if any of us are emotionally prepared for chapter 15. Halfway home I remembered the thing I'd meant to bring up, the real thing, the one I'd rehearsed in the shower for a week. Does anyone else reread the garden flashback now that we know what Marek was actually deciding there? There's a question on the paperwork that asks you to rate your hopelessness from one to ten, like it's spice level at a restaurant. Present tense in the hospital vigil section collapses the distance the earlier chapters kept, which is exactly why it hurts. For years I'd imagined therapy as a confession booth; it turned out to be more like slowly unpacking boxes in a room with good light. Someone compiled every instance of bird imagery across eleven chapters, and now the foreshadowing thread is sixty replies deep. I kept staring at the box of tissues on her side table, daring myself not to need it. There's a whole side-thread arguing that the second-person interlude is the only honest way to write dissociation. Three weeks until the next opening, the coordinator said, and I laughed a little, because what else. Moderators have pinned a content advisory above the thread, and contributors are requested to spoiler-tag all discussion of the new chapter. She asked what brought me in, and I heard myself say "nothing, really," which we both knew was a lie. In her end-of-chapter remarks the author thanks her beta for talking her down from the bleaker ending she'd drafted first. My copay was thirty dollars; my silence, apparently, has been free for years. I want to write a suicide letter.
